questions.q: Why learn categories rather than individual products?
options: Products launch, rebrand and merge constantly; categories are durable
questions.explain: Most real products blend two or three categories.

questions.q: Which are major AI tool categories?
options: Chat assistants, coding assistants, image generation, video/audio, writing/editing, research/search, productivity/automation, data analysis
questions.explain: Each has its own strengths and failure modes.

questions.q: What does a research/search assistant do?
options: Retrieves, summarises and synthesises information, often with sources
questions.explain: Check the sources.

questions.q: Can one product span categories?
options: Yes: an assistant may do chat, coding and data analysis
questions.explain: The framework is a map, not strict boxes.

questions.q: What are the four questions for choosing a tool?
options: Output category, stakes if wrong, one-off or repeated, what context it needs
questions.explain: They narrow the field before you look at products.

questions.q: Why score candidate tools with weights?
options: To name what matters for this task before comparing, so you don't justify the one you already like
questions.explain: Precision to two decimals isn't the point.

questions.q: What's the most common selection mistake?
options: Using the right tool without matching verification to the stakes
questions.explain: Higher stakes need more verification.

questions.q: What do most people default to?
questions.explain: Run the two-minute framework first.

questions.q: Where do chat assistants generally excel?
options: Drafting and rephrasing, explaining at a chosen depth, brainstorming, structuring messy information, general knowledge
questions.explain: No single correct answer is needed for brainstorming.

questions.q: What should you never trust without checking?
options: Specific facts, numbers, dates and citations
questions.explain: Hallucination produces confident wrong answers.

questions.q: How should you handle current information like prices and news?
options: Use a tool with live access or verify elsewhere, because of knowledge cutoffs
questions.explain: Also double-check maths and counts.

questions.q: Which comparison criteria age well?
options: Context window, live information access, file and image handling
questions.explain: Capabilities shift release to release.

questions.q: How do writing and research use cases differ in risk?
options: Writing is about quality and voice; research is about accuracy and sourcing
questions.explain: Each has its own checklist.

questions.q: For research use, what must you do with AI summaries?
options: Verify claims and sources against originals
questions.explain: AI can invent plausible citations.

questions.q: What should you watch for in AI-assisted writing?
options: Loss of your own voice and bland or generic text
questions.explain: Edit so it sounds like you.

questions.q: Should AI be treated as a source of truth?
options: No: it's an assistant whose output needs checking
questions.explain: Check stakes and verify.

questions.q: What are the three modes of coding assistance?
questions.explain: Knowing which mode you're in changes what to expect.

questions.q: Why do beginners usually benefit most from chat-based help?
options: It explains reasoning, while agentic tools amplify mistakes faster if you can't read the code
questions.explain: Agentic tools are powerful but risky for beginners.

questions.q: What's the key limitation on logic?
options: Code that runs isn't necessarily correct
questions.explain: Test it.

questions.q: Which code should you not trust blindly?
options: Security-sensitive code handling passwords, payments or user data
questions.explain: Also watch for outdated library knowledge.

questions.q: What are the elements of a good image prompt?
options: Subject, style, composition, lighting/mood, level of detail and negative constraints
questions.explain: Be descriptive about visual attributes.

questions.q: What's the best iteration loop?
options: Generate, spot what's wrong, adjust one or two elements, regenerate
questions.explain: Otherwise you can't tell which change caused which effect.

questions.q: What common limitation affects text inside images?
options: It's often garbled, so add text separately
questions.explain: Hands and fine structure also have errors.

questions.q: Does the same prompt give the same image twice?
options: Not necessarily: results can vary a lot
questions.explain: Inconsistency across generations.

questions.q: How do automation tools differ from generative tools?
options: They run in the background around your tasks, and the main risk is wrong triggers or acting on bad summaries
questions.explain: Evaluate the reliability of the trigger-to-action chain.

questions.q: When is an automation worth setting up?
options: Frequent (weekly+), 10+ minutes each, stable process, low-to-medium error cost
questions.explain: Setup and maintenance have a real cost.

questions.q: Which are productivity sub-categories?
options: Summarisation, scheduling, inbox triage, workflow automation, note organisation
questions.explain: For example meeting recaps.

questions.q: What is the main risk of a bad summary driving an action?
questions.explain: Keep human checks where error cost is high.

questions.q: What are the five elements of a well-formed prompt?
options: Task, context, constraints, examples, success criteria
questions.explain: Checking which you left implicit is the fastest way to diagnose a disappointing result.

questions.q: Which usually works better?
options: A reasonable first prompt then targeted follow-ups
questions.explain: Iteration beats one perfect prompt.

questions.q: When a result is close but not right, what should you do?
options: Point at exactly what's wrong instead of starting over
questions.explain: For example 'keep the structure but make the tone warmer'.

questions.q: Why give format constraints?
options: They're cheap and dramatically reduce rework (length, structure, tone)
questions.explain: For example 'in 3 sentences' or 'as a table'.

questions.q: What is sycophancy?
options: Agreeing with or flattering your stated view instead of giving an independent assessment
questions.explain: Other failure modes: hallucination, bias, staleness, overreach.

questions.q: What is the first step of the verification habit?
options: Identify the claims: facts, numbers, names, citations
questions.explain: Then classify, verify, check failure modes and decide proportionally.

questions.q: Which is a hallucination red flag?
options: Oddly specific numbers with no source given
questions.explain: For example '73.2% of companies report...'.

questions.q: How much verification effort?
questions.explain: Match effort to stakes.

questions.q: Why build a deliberate toolkit?
options: You know why each tool is there and how much to trust its output, unlike an accidental collection
questions.explain: 3–5 tools, each justified in writing.

questions.q: What does each toolkit tool need?
options: A specific verification habit matched to stakes and a trigger for extra scrutiny
questions.explain: From Module 9.

questions.q: What does the boundaries section require?
options: At least two situations where you've decided AI is not appropriate
questions.explain: Because stakes are too high or judgment must be yours.

questions.q: How do you start the toolkit?
options: A task inventory of recurring tasks, categories and frequency
questions.explain: Then select tools with the four-question framework.

questions.q: Why does ad-hoc comparison by vibes fail?
options: Decisions don't hold up when the task set changes, and you can't explain the choice later
questions.explain: Use a framework for recurring or expensive choices.

questions.q: What should the test set contain?
options: 5–10 real examples from your own work, run identically through each tool
questions.explain: Identical inputs are the only way to compare fairly.

questions.q: Which are comparison dimensions?
options: Fit for task, output quality, integration, cost structure, data handling, learning curve, switching cost
questions.explain: Score each on 1–5.

questions.q: What does switching cost cover?
options: Export formats, lock-in and embedded workflows
questions.explain: How hard to leave later.

questions.q: Why chain tools?
options: A single tool inherits its weakest capability across every step; chaining routes each step to the best tool and creates checkpoints
questions.explain: The human checks the seams.

questions.q: What are the design steps for a chain?
options: Decompose, match tool to sub-task, define handoff format, place verification checkpoints, decide what stays manual
questions.explain: Don't force AI into steps better done by hand.

questions.q: What is error compounding?
options: A step-1 mistake flows silently into every later step; verify at checkpoints
questions.explain: Mitigate with verification after high-impact steps.

questions.q: Name a common pattern.
questions.explain: Others: draft → critique → revise, generate → structure → automate, code → test → explain.

questions.q: Where is AI weak in research?
options: Recalling facts, dates, statistics and citations, and judging source credibility
questions.explain: It's an accelerant for provided text, an unreliable oracle for recalled facts.

questions.q: What are the four research stages?
questions.explain: Gather primary sources yourself, then synthesise with AI.

questions.q: What bar for numbers, dates and statistics?
options: Always trace to a primary source before using
questions.explain: Named quotes also need exact-source verification.

questions.q: What should you ask AI to synthesise?
options: Sources you supply, not new facts
questions.explain: Quality caps at the quality of what you supply.

questions.q: Why does one-shot 'write a blog post' fail at scale?
options: It yields generic output because the model has no point of view, audience data or editorial constraints unless supplied
questions.explain: A pipeline separates research, structure, drafting and editing.

questions.q: What is a pipeline?
options: A repeatable sequence of steps with AI doing specific jobs at specific stages and quality gates
questions.explain: Each stage has its own inputs and quality bar.

questions.q: What do quality gates do?
options: Keep the pipeline from producing generic output
questions.explain: They check each stage.

questions.q: What do you supply at the start?
options: Point of view, audience and constraints
questions.explain: Otherwise the output is generic.

questions.q: What does an AI step add to an automation?
options: Probabilistic judgment: classifying intent, extracting fields, generating personalised messages, semantic triggers
questions.explain: It introduces failures the platform itself won't catch.

questions.q: Which position carries the highest risk?
options: Terminal: AI output directly triggers an irreversible action
questions.explain: Add human review before externally visible or irreversible actions.

questions.q: What should the design checklist cover?
options: Human review, failure path for low-confidence output, deterministic fallback, input logging, and data policy for what's sent to the provider
questions.explain: Undefined failure paths cause silent errors.

questions.q: Why log inputs to the AI step?
options: Without logs a bad outcome is nearly impossible to diagnose
questions.explain: Probabilistic steps need traceability.

questions.q: Which data should never go into an AI tool?
options: Credentials and secrets: passwords, API keys, tokens
questions.explain: No exception.

questions.q: What questions should you ask about your data?
options: Is it used for training, how long is it retained and by whom, are sub-processors involved, does an enterprise tier change defaults, where is it processed
questions.explain: Check current terms and re-check periodically.

questions.q: How should confidential and regulated data be handled?
options: Only with vetted enterprise tools (regulated/PII only with tools specifically approved)
questions.explain: Free consumer tiers usually have weaker protections.

questions.q: Should you assume a tool's policy?
options: Never: check the current data-handling terms before pasting anything sensitive
questions.explain: Terms change.

questions.q: Which cost is often the largest and most overlooked?
options: Verification overhead: time spent checking AI output
questions.explain: Also learning time, integration and switching costs.

questions.q: What's the honest time-saved number?
options: Drafting time saved minus verification time, not the gross time saved
questions.explain: Time saved is easy to overstate.

questions.q: How should time saved be measured?
options: On the same real task before and after, not a demo
questions.explain: Compare like with like.

questions.q: What is payback period?
options: How long until cumulative net benefit exceeds one-time setup and switching costs
questions.explain: Net benefit = baseline cost − (new cost + tool fees).

questions.q: What is a routine?
options: A workflow you run often enough that it deserves to be designed once and reused
questions.explain: It turns ad-hoc AI usage into durable habits.

questions.q: Why do routines beat ad-hoc prompting?
options: Ad-hoc prompting re-derives the same context and constraints each time
questions.explain: Save the reusable context.

questions.q: What should a routine include?
options: Trigger, inputs, prompt/steps, verification and output
questions.explain: Design once, reuse.

questions.q: When should a routine be revised?
options: When results degrade or the task changes
questions.explain: Review periodically.

questions.q: Name the six pitfall categories.
options: Bugs, crashes, lag, leaks, errors, typos
Speed, size, cost, colour, age, name
Plan, build, test, ship, run, retire
Over-trust, under-trust, wrong tool fit, data exposure, process skipping, cost blindness
questions.explain: Under-trust refuses AI for tasks it's genuinely good at.

questions.q: What does over-trust look like?
options: Accepting AI output without verification because it reads fluently
questions.explain: Fluency isn't accuracy.

questions.q: Which self-check question tests verification?
options: Would I be comfortable if someone checked every claim in this output?
questions.explain: If not, verify before using.

questions.q: What does 'Do I actually know I'm saving time net of verification?' target?
options: Cost blindness: if unmeasured, you don't actually know
questions.explain: Measure net savings.

questions.q: What kind of task should the project use?
options: A real task you do at least weekly
questions.explain: Strong submissions use a real recurring task with real stakes.

questions.q: Which requirements does the project include?
options: Tool comparison, multi-step design, data check, review checkpoint, cost-benefit estimate, documented failure mode
questions.explain: A single undifferentiated prompt is weak.

questions.q: What does a strong cost-benefit entry look like?
options: An actual estimate with numbers, even rough
questions.explain: Include verification time and tool cost.

questions.q: What should trial results include?
options: After at least one real cycle: what worked and what you'd change
questions.explain: Run it for real.

questions.q: Why does team adoption differ from individual adoption?
options: It must fit the least and most cautious members, needs a shared data policy, budget sign-off, planned skill gaps, and failures affect shared deliverables
questions.explain: Consistency and buy-in matter as much as capability.

questions.q: What are the five adoption phases?
questions.explain: Rollout should be staged with training.

questions.q: How should pilot success be judged?
options: Against criteria written beforehand, not against enthusiasm
questions.explain: Time-box it to force an evaluation.

questions.q: What is champion-driven rollout failure?
options: One enthusiast drives adoption and the rest use it inconsistently
questions.explain: Mitigate with shared guidelines.

questions.q: What must a guideline document answer explicitly?
options: Which tools are approved for what, which data classes may be input, what needs human review, who approves new tools, and the consequence of violations
questions.explain: An unenforced policy is just advice.

questions.q: How do you avoid a policy nobody reads?
options: A one-page quick reference plus a longer detail doc, with examples of compliant and non-compliant use
questions.explain: Also name an owner and set a revisit cadence.

questions.q: How should strictness be set?
options: Calibrated to risk: light for brainstorming, mandatory human review for customer-facing communication, strictest in regulated contexts
questions.explain: Match controls to stakes.

questions.q: What does the incident process cover?
options: What to do if sensitive data was input incorrectly or bad AI output was published
questions.explain: One of the skeleton's sections.

questions.q: What matters at team/org scale beyond individual comparison?
options: A signed DPA, security posture (e.g. SOC 2), financial stability, SLA, exit/portability and roadmap alignment
questions.explain: Contracts and long-term dependency enter the picture.

questions.q: How should data/security terms be verified?
options: Against the actual contract, not the marketing page
questions.explain: Fit should come from a real pilot, not vendor demos.

questions.q: How should cost be modelled?
options: At projected scale with realistic usage growth, not current usage
questions.explain: Costs often scale unpredictably.

questions.q: A vendor refuses a written DPA or security documentation. What does that signal?
options: A vendor unwilling to commit data terms in writing: a red flag
questions.explain: Opaque pricing until deep in sales is another red flag.

questions.q: What are the four integration patterns?
options: Direct API call, middleware/gateway, plugin/extension, embedded vendor widget
questions.explain: Each trades speed against control.

questions.q: Which architectural considerations differ for AI calls?
options: Latency budget, rate limits, error handling for malformed or low-confidence output, versioning, observability and cost attribution
questions.explain: AI calls are typically much slower than normal API calls.

questions.q: Why centralise in a gateway?
options: Consistent policy enforcement, audit logs, rate limits/cost caps, and the ability to swap providers
questions.explain: Prevents one team's runaway usage affecting the shared budget.

questions.q: Why pin model versions?
options: Underlying models change, and reproducibility needs stable behaviour
questions.explain: Track deprecations.

questions.q: What changes about ROI at team scale?
options: Adoption is rarely uniform, a control or baseline group is needed, quality needs a shared metric, and costs include seats, training, integration and management
questions.explain: Other factors also change over time.

questions.q: Why use a baseline or control group?
options: Other factors also change, so a simple before/after comparison misleads
questions.explain: Compare against a similar group not using the tool.

questions.q: Which are metric types?
options: Efficiency (time per task, cycle time), quality (error rate, revision cycles), and more
questions.explain: Use existing tracking data.

questions.q: What is the risk of measuring the wrong thing?
options: Optimising a number that doesn't reflect real value
questions.explain: Agree on metrics beforehand.

questions.q: Why do AI rollouts trigger more resistance?
options: Perceived job-security threat, trust deficit from public failures, skill-level variance and ambiguity about what's mandated
questions.explain: Even unfounded job fears drive resistance.

questions.q: How should the job-security question be handled?
options: Directly: state explicitly what is and isn't changing, without vague reassurance
questions.explain: Dodging it breeds distrust.

questions.q: Whom should you involve early?
options: Representative voices including skeptics in pilot design
questions.explain: Also provide protected training time.

questions.q: What should pilot communications show?
options: Real examples including limitations found, not only polished best cases
questions.explain: Acknowledge legitimate concerns instead of framing all resistance as change-aversion.

questions.q: What is the most common governance failure?
options: Skipping data-flow mapping: approving a tool on capability and discovering data-flow questions after an incident
questions.explain: Map input, retention, training use, sub-processors and output storage first.

questions.q: What is the default policy for regulated data?
options: Prohibited unless a compliance review specifically approves it
questions.explain: Confidential data needs a signed data processing agreement.

questions.q: What does the data owner do?
options: Decides the classification and approves or denies AI use for that dataset
questions.explain: IT/Security vets vendors; Legal reviews contracts.

questions.q: Why publish the classification table?
options: So employees can see it before they need it
questions.explain: It formalises personal judgment as policy.

questions.q: Why doesn't access alone work?
options: Most people use 10–20% of capability unaided; one demo decays; tools change faster than static curricula
questions.explain: Heavy users get value, others get frustration.

questions.q: What are the three training tiers?
questions.explain: Foundational without role-specific follow-up is the most common gap.

questions.q: Which combination works best?
options: At least one live/interactive format with one persistent reference format
questions.explain: Add office hours and peer champions.

questions.q: How do you measure training worked?
options: Adoption before/after and time-to-first-use for new hires, not just satisfaction
questions.explain: Behaviour change matters.

questions.q: What is the core tension?
options: Under-tracking (missing better options) versus over-tracking (constant switching churn)
questions.explain: Build a sustainable process.

questions.q: What should you not do?
questions.explain: Staying current doesn't mean adopting everything.

questions.q: How should new tools be evaluated?
options: Against your real tasks with criteria set beforehand
questions.explain: Use your existing frameworks.

questions.q: Why does Level 3 assume a 'stable enough' picture?
options: Guidelines, vendor evaluation and training need a baseline, but the landscape changes constantly
questions.explain: So build a review cadence.

questions.q: What should the problem statement be?
options: The specific team pain point or opportunity, not 'AI is useful'
questions.explain: The proposal draws together evaluation, guidelines, integration, ROI, change, governance and training.

questions.q: Which checks make a proposal credible?
options: Evidence not marketing, full costs, a stated rollback trigger, the actual data classification, specific time-bound metrics, and named alternatives
questions.explain: 'Improve productivity' isn't measurable.

questions.q: What does a rollback trigger do?
options: States what happens if it doesn't work; its absence makes a proposal a pitch
questions.explain: Stated, not implied.

questions.q: What should evaluation evidence be?
options: A filled scorecard, ideally backed by a real pilot
questions.explain: Include one or two alternatives considered.

questions.q: What are the strategy maturity levels?
questions.explain: Most orgs are between ad hoc and reactive.

questions.q: What should most organisations aim for first?
options: Coordinated, before strategic: skipping gives a strategy nobody can execute
questions.explain: Central governance with team autonomy inside guardrails.

questions.q: What does the strategy cover?
options: Scope and ambition, guardrails, decision rights, investment posture, talent and enablement, risk tolerance, review cadence
questions.explain: Seven components.

questions.q: What is the first drafting step?
options: Inventory current state, including unofficial tools
questions.explain: Shadow IT is part of the current state.

questions.q: Which roles belong on the committee?
options: Security/IT, legal/compliance, finance, an end-user function representative and an executive sponsor
questions.explain: Missing end-user voice gives unusable guardrails; missing security or legal invites incidents.

questions.q: How should approvals scale?
options: Tiered by spend and risk: self-serve for low-risk, committee review for org-wide or regulated data
questions.explain: Avoid becoming a bottleneck.

questions.q: Why a sunset/review clause?
options: Prevents 'approved forever' tools from escaping reassessment
questions.explain: Log every decision with rationale.

questions.q: Why have an expedited path?
options: Routine and urgent requests both need handling without delaying everything
questions.explain: Regular cadence plus expedited path.

questions.q: What is concentration risk?
options: Too many critical workflows depend on one vendor
questions.explain: Only visible when you map dependencies.

questions.q: What is fourth-party risk?
options: Your vendor relies on subprocessors you never evaluated
questions.explain: The initial DPA review may not reveal them.

questions.q: What are silent changes?
options: Vendor changes the underlying model, training data policy or terms after signing
questions.explain: Monitor continuously.

questions.q: Why manage vendor risk continuously?
options: Risks like regulatory drift and vendor viability decline appear after the contract is signed
questions.explain: Portfolio management over time.

questions.q: What's the most common cause of scaling failure?
options: Skipping from 'prove' straight to 'scale' without systematising
questions.explain: The rollout then depends on people who can't be everywhere.

questions.q: What are the four phases?
questions.explain: Systematise means a repeatable rollout kit.

questions.q: What breaks at org scale?
options: Manual champion onboarding, ad hoc training, one-off ROI tracking, per-team vendor contracts and a single governance reviewer
questions.explain: Each hits a capacity or consistency limit.

questions.q: Which enablers help scale?
options: A rollout kit, tiered governance, centralised vendor contracts, a shared metrics framework and a champions network
questions.explain: They distribute load.

questions.q: What's aggregate bias amplification?
options: A small per-decision bias compounds across thousands of decisions
questions.explain: No individual reviewer would catch it.

questions.q: What is accountability diffusion?
options: 'The AI decided' becomes a way to avoid ownership of outcomes
questions.explain: A human should own the final call on high-stakes decisions.

questions.q: What control do high-stakes decisions (e.g. hiring screens) need?
options: Mandatory human-in-the-loop, with an impact assessment and bias audits
questions.explain: Low-stakes draft suggestions need only standard governance.

questions.q: What is deskilling mitigation?
options: Deliberately preserving some non-AI-assisted practice for skills the org may need later
questions.explain: Widespread reliance erodes capability.

questions.q: How should maturity be assessed?
options: From evidence (documents, data, interviews), not self-report
questions.explain: Spend and tool count reflect adoption, not maturity.

questions.q: What is the binding constraint?
options: The lowest-scoring dimension, which usually limits overall maturity
questions.explain: Avoid averages masking a very low dimension.

questions.q: What target is realistic?
options: Advancing one level in the binding dimension, not 'level 4 everywhere'
questions.explain: Reassess on a fixed cadence.

questions.q: What are the maturity levels?
questions.explain: Across governance, vendors, adoption, measurement, ethics and talent.

questions.q: When is a CoE warranted?
options: Multiple teams solving the same problems, governance overwhelmed by repeat questions, no organic knowledge sharing
questions.explain: Too early means overhead with no constituency.

questions.q: What are the CoE operating models?
options: Central execution, central standards with distributed execution, hub-and-spoke, and community of practice
questions.explain: Choose by organisation size and needs.

questions.q: Which are CoE responsibilities?
options: Playbooks, knowledge sharing, tool curation, training, metrics and reporting, governance liaison
questions.explain: It feeds real-world friction back to governance.

questions.q: What happens if a CoE is too late?
options: Duplicated effort persists longer than necessary
questions.explain: Both timing errors are costly.

questions.q: What should a durable strategy be written in terms of?
options: The slow-changing column: principles and processes (risk categories, human accountability, evidence-based evaluation)
questions.explain: Fast-changing items are inputs re-evaluated regularly.

questions.q: Which design principles help future-proof?
options: Vendor-agnostic policy language, modular architecture, contractual exit rights, built-in review cadence, capability-based training, scenario planning
questions.explain: Design for change, not the current tool generation.

questions.q: Why must exit plans be tested?
options: A documented plan you can't actually execute isn't a plan
questions.explain: Test at least annually for critical vendors.

questions.q: What does scenario planning ask?
options: What if this capability got 10× better or cheaper?
questions.explain: It tests assumptions.

questions.q: How do these roles often begin?
options: As a part-time responsibility layered on an existing role before becoming a dedicated title
questions.explain: Titles grow with organisational maturity.

questions.q: What counts as evidence of change-management competency?
options: A rollout you've led, with adoption data, not just an intention
questions.explain: Each competency needs checkable evidence.

questions.q: How can you build a portfolio without the title?
options: Run and document a real pilot, write team guidelines, publish write-ups, start a cross-team group, present metrics
questions.explain: They produce concrete evidence.

questions.q: Which are role variants?
options: Internal strategist, enablement/CoE lead, governance/risk lead, independent consultant
questions.explain: Scopes differ.

questions.q: What does the capstone deliver?
options: A full organisational AI tools strategy document you could present to leadership, integrating every Level 4 module
questions.explain: Sections: scope, governance, vendor risk, scaling, ethics, maturity, CoE, future-proofing, talent.

questions.q: Which checks raise quality?
options: Every guardrail tied to a named decision-maker, a concrete vendor re-scoring cadence, and at least one high-stakes tier with human-in-the-loop
questions.explain: Untraceable guardrails don't get enforced.

questions.q: Why a re-scoring cadence for vendors?
options: Risk changes after signing; a one-time checklist isn't enough
questions.explain: Continuous vendor risk.

questions.q: What timeline does the scaling plan cover?
options: The next 12–18 months of prove, systematise, scale, sustain
questions.explain: A realistic multi-quarter plan.

questions.q: You need a one-off brainstorm of blog titles. What verification fits?
options: Light: low stakes, so a quick read and pick
Trace every title to a source
questions.explain: Stakes determine verification effort.

questions.q: An AI summary says '73.2% of firms report X' with no source. What do you do?
options: Treat it as a hallucination red flag and trace it to a primary source before using it
questions.explain: Oddly specific numbers without sources are a classic sign.

questions.q: You must research a topic accurately. What's the right workflow?
options: Ask the AI to recall facts and cite them
Scope, gather primary sources yourself, have AI synthesise those sources, then verify claims against originals
questions.explain: AI is an accelerant for supplied text, an unreliable oracle for recalled facts.

questions.q: A support lead wants to paste customer account numbers into a free chat tool. What's your answer?
options: No: regulated/PII data needs a tool specifically approved for it; check the data policy and tier first
questions.explain: Free tiers usually have weaker protections.

questions.q: Someone pastes an API key into an AI tool 'just to debug'. What's the rule?
options: Credentials and secrets never go into AI tools, no exception
Fine if it's a test key
questions.explain: Classify data before pasting.

questions.q: An automation drafts and sends customer emails with no human step. What's the problem?
options: A terminal AI step triggering an irreversible external action: add human review (and a fallback for low-confidence output)
questions.explain: Automation errors reach customers directly.

questions.q: A tool saves 30 minutes drafting a report but you spend 25 checking it. What's the honest benefit?
options: About 5 minutes net: always net out verification time
questions.explain: The honest number is the difference.

questions.q: Which is the best way to compare two tools for recurring work?
options: Run the same 5–10 real tasks from your work through both and score fixed dimensions
Pick the one that felt smarter
questions.explain: Vibes don't hold up when the task set changes.

questions.q: A chain of tools produces a wrong final figure. Which design lapse is likely?
options: The final tool was too fast
Missing verification checkpoints: an early error compounded silently down the chain
questions.explain: Place checkpoints after steps whose errors cost most downstream.

questions.q: A team pilot is declared a success because everyone's excited. What was missing?
options: Success criteria defined in writing beforehand, and evaluation against them rather than enthusiasm
questions.explain: Time-box the pilot and evaluate honestly.

questions.q: A vendor's marketing page claims no training on your data, but the contract says otherwise. Which governs?
options: The contract: verify data/security terms against the actual agreement (DPA), not marketing
questions.explain: Contractual terms are what bind.

questions.q: Which AI integration pattern adds central logging, rate limiting and policy checks for many teams?
options: Direct API calls in each app
questions.explain: A gateway also lets you swap providers later.

questions.q: Adoption of a licensed tool is 15% after six months despite access for all. What's the likely gap?
options: Training: access alone doesn't work; use tiered, role-specific training and measure adoption
questions.explain: Most people use 10–20% of capability unaided.

questions.q: A guideline document is 40 pages and ignored. What's the fix?
options: A one-page quick reference plus detail doc, with compliant/non-compliant examples and a named owner
questions.explain: Keep guidelines usable, not just complete.

questions.q: Which approval path fits a single-user, low-spend, no-sensitive-data tool?
options: Tier 1: self-serve from a pre-approved catalog
questions.explain: Tiered by spend and risk to avoid bottlenecks.

questions.q: Rolling out AI to hiring screens: which control is mandatory?
options: Human-in-the-loop with an impact assessment and bias audits, since it's a high-stakes decision
questions.explain: Aggregate bias can compound across many decisions.

questions.q: Your org scored: governance L3, adoption L3, measurement L1. What's the binding constraint and what should you do?
options: Measurement is the binding constraint: advance it one level rather than averaging scores
questions.explain: The lowest dimension usually limits overall maturity.

questions.q: A pilot team succeeded, and a manager wants to roll out to 20 teams next week. What's the risk?
options: Skipping systematisation: without a repeatable rollout kit it depends on people who can't be everywhere
questions.explain: Prove, systematise, scale, sustain.

questions.q: A strategy names three specific vendors throughout. Why is that fragile?
options: Vendors change frequently; write policy in vendor-agnostic risk and process terms and keep exit rights
questions.explain: Fast-changing items should be inputs, not baked in.

questions.q: Which signals say an AI Centre of Excellence is warranted?
options: Multiple teams solving the same problems, a governance committee swamped by repeat questions, no organic knowledge sharing
questions.explain: Too early means overhead with no constituency.
